examples: She certainly knows how to throw a party.
It's certainly not the cheapest option, but it's the best.
Things will certainly get busier after the holidays.
“Could you help me with this box?” “Certainly.”
“Can I pay by card?” “Certainly — right over here.”
“May I borrow your car tonight?” “Certainly not.”

senses.head: Without any doubt; definitely
examples: She certainly knows how to throw a party.
It's certainly not the cheapest option, but it's the best.
Things will certainly get busier after the holidays.

senses.head: Used as a polite answer to agree or give permission: yes, of course; certainly not is a firm no
examples: “Could you help me with this box?” “Certainly.”
“Can I pay by card?” “Certainly — right over here.”
“May I borrow your car tonight?” “Certainly not.”

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also alone as an answer
entries.contrast: Surely is not a synonym: Certainly he knows states a fact, but Surely you know him means “I'd be amazed if you didn't” and asks for agreement. As a reply, Certainly is polite and a little formal; everyday American speech says Sure.

examples: I'm definitely coming to your party.
That was definitely the best pizza I've ever had.
We definitely need more chairs for Saturday.
“Are you going to vote?” “Definitely.”
“Would you go back to that hotel?” “Definitely not.”
Nothing has been definitely decided yet.
We can't say definitely when the store will reopen.

senses.head: Without any doubt; for sure
examples: I'm definitely coming to your party.
That was definitely the best pizza I've ever had.
We definitely need more chairs for Saturday.

senses.head: Used as an answer to say a strong yes or no
examples: “Are you going to vote?” “Definitely.”
“Would you go back to that hotel?” “Definitely not.”

senses.head: In a fixed, final way, so that there is no more doubt or change
examples: Nothing has been definitely decided yet.
We can't say definitely when the store will reopen.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also alone as an answer
entries.contrast: Order with not changes the meaning: It's definitely not true = точно неправда, but It's not definitely true = не факт, что правда. Do not use it for Russian определённый = “certain, particular”: в определённой степени is to a certain extent, not definitely to some degree.

examples: Obviously, we can't leave the kids home alone.
“Did you tell her?” “Obviously not.”
We'll obviously pay you back as soon as we can.
She was obviously upset about something.
He'd obviously never cooked a turkey before.
The dog was obviously hungry.

senses.head: Used to say that something is clear or expected and should need no explanation
examples: Obviously, we can't leave the kids home alone.
“Did you tell her?” “Obviously not.”
We'll obviously pay you back as soon as we can.

senses.head: In a way that is easy to see or notice
examples: She was obviously upset about something.
He'd obviously never cooked a turkey before.
The dog was obviously hungry.

entries.type: stance — what everyone should know; also manner
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian очевидно often means “probably, it seems” (Очевидно, он опоздал на поезд) — that is apparently or evidently in English. Obviously means “as anyone can see” and can sound rude if the listener did not know: Obviously, the meeting is at three.

examples: The owners had evidently left in a hurry.
Evidently, nobody told him about the schedule change.
“Did the package come?” “Evidently not.”
He was evidently nervous — his hands were shaking.
She was evidently pleased with the results.

senses.head: Based on what you can see or have found out; apparently
examples: The owners had evidently left in a hurry.
Evidently, nobody told him about the schedule change.
“Did the package come?” “Evidently not.”

senses.head: In a way that is plain to see; clearly
examples: He was evidently nervous — his hands were shaking.
She was evidently pleased with the results.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.contrast: Evidently is closer to Russian очевидно, по-видимому (a conclusion) than obviously is. It is a little more formal than apparently, and like apparently it can also pass on what the speaker has heard: Evidently, she quit last week = судя по всему (говорят), она уволилась.

examples: Apparently, the restaurant is closing next month.
He's apparently moving to Denver.
The meeting got canceled, apparently.
The back door had apparently been forced open.
It started as an apparently harmless joke.

senses.head: According to what you have heard or read, though you cannot be sure
examples: Apparently, the restaurant is closing next month.
He's apparently moving to Denver.
The meeting got canceled, apparently.

senses.head: Seeming to be true from what you can see, though it may not be
examples: The back door had apparently been forced open.
It started as an apparently harmless joke.

entries.type: stance — what the speaker has heard or what seems true
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma, and end in speech
entries.contrast: False friend: apparently does not mean явно, очевидно. The adjective can (for no apparent reason = без видимой причины), but the adverb almost always means “I heard” or “it seems”: Apparently he's rich = говорят, он богат.

entries.meaning: Used to say that you think something is very likely true, based on what you know. ---
examples: You're presumably tired after such a long flight.
Presumably, the package will arrive tomorrow.
He left early, presumably to beat the traffic.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.contrast: Presumably is the speaker's own reasonable guess, which they expect to be right. Russian news style предположительно (предположительно, преступник) is allegedly or suspected in English, not presumably.

entries.meaning: Very likely; more likely than not. ---
examples: It'll probably rain this afternoon.
She probably won't remember me.
“Are you coming tonight?” “Probably.”
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary, and before a negative auxiliary (probably won't)
entries.contrast: Position with a negative: He probably won't come, not He won't probably come. Russian наверное is often a polite hedge; probably really means “more likely than not”, so I'll probably come is a weak promise.

examples: The drive could take three hours, possibly more.
It was possibly the worst movie I've ever seen.
“Will you finish today?” “Possibly.”
I can't possibly eat all that.
How could anyone possibly believe him?
We did everything we possibly could.
Could you possibly turn the music down a little?
Could I possibly borrow your notes from Tuesday?

senses.head: Perhaps; used when something could be true but is not certain
examples: The drive could take three hours, possibly more.
It was possibly the worst movie I've ever seen.
“Will you finish today?” “Possibly.”

senses.head: Used with can or could for emphasis: in any way at all
examples: I can't possibly eat all that.
How could anyone possibly believe him?
We did everything we possibly could.

senses.head: Used to make a request more polite
examples: Could you possibly turn the music down a little?
Could I possibly borrow your notes from Tuesday?

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after the modal (can't possibly); also alone as an answer
entries.contrast: Can't possibly is not “maybe can't” — it means “there is no way”: I can't possibly finish by Friday = я никак не успею к пятнице. In a request, Could you possibly…? is extra polite, not doubtful.

examples: Maybe she's stuck in traffic.
We could go to the beach, or maybe the lake.
“Are you coming with us?” “Maybe.”
Maybe we should call a plumber.
Maybe you could ask your dad for help.
There were maybe fifty people at the meeting.
It's maybe a ten-minute walk from here.

senses.head: Perhaps; possibly
examples: Maybe she's stuck in traffic.
We could go to the beach, or maybe the lake.
“Are you coming with us?” “Maybe.”

senses.head: Used to make a suggestion politely
examples: Maybe we should call a plumber.
Maybe you could ask your dad for help.

senses.head: Used before a number: about, approximately
examples: There were maybe fifty people at the meeting.
It's maybe a ten-minute walk from here.

entries.position: front — usually at the start of the clause; also before a number, and alone as an answer
entries.contrast: Maybe (one word) is the adverb; may be (two words) is a modal and a verb: Maybe he is right = He may be right. Never He maybe right. Maybe is informal; in writing perhaps is more common.

examples: Perhaps the letter got lost in the mail.
It was perhaps the most important decision of her career.
“Will he agree?” “Perhaps.”
Perhaps you'd like to wait in the lobby.
Perhaps we could discuss this after lunch?
Perhaps two hundred people showed up.
The house is perhaps a mile from the highway.

senses.head: Possibly; maybe
examples: Perhaps the letter got lost in the mail.
It was perhaps the most important decision of her career.
“Will he agree?” “Perhaps.”

senses.head: Used to make a suggestion, offer or request more polite
examples: Perhaps you'd like to wait in the lobby.
Perhaps we could discuss this after lunch?

senses.head: Used before a number: about, approximately
examples: Perhaps two hundred people showed up.
The house is perhaps a mile from the highway.

entries.position: front — at the start of the clause; also mid, especially before an adjective or noun phrase
entries.contrast: Perhaps is more formal than maybe; in everyday American conversation maybe is far more common. Unlike maybe, perhaps sits easily in mid position: It was perhaps her best book.

examples: She is undoubtedly the best player on the team.
Prices will undoubtedly go up again next year.
Undoubtedly, the new law will be challenged in court.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.form: un- + doubted + -ly; the b is silent and the -ed is a full syllable
entries.contrast: Undoubtedly means full certainty; doubtless, despite its look, often means only “probably”.

entries.meaning: Used to say that something can reasonably be claimed, and the speaker believes it, though others may disagree. ---
examples: He is arguably the greatest basketball player of all time.
It was arguably the most important invention of the century.
Arguably, the city's best food is found in its smallest restaurants.
entries.type: stance — a claim the speaker supports
entries.position: mid — usually right before the adjective or noun phrase it comments on; also front with a comma
entries.contrast: False friend: the adjective arguable often means “спорный”, but arguably supports the claim — He is arguably the best = пожалуй, он лучший (and the speaker thinks so). It is not doubt and not доказуемо.

entries.meaning: According to what someone has said, especially in an accusation that has not been proved. ---
examples: The suspect allegedly stole more than $10,000 from his employer.
He was allegedly driving over 90 miles an hour.
The company allegedly hid the test results from regulators.
entries.type: stance — a claim that has not been proved
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary
entries.form: -ly from alleged; the -ed is a full syllable
entries.contrast: In news reports allegedly protects the writer: someone has made the claim, usually an accusation, but it is not proved. It is not the speaker's own guess — that is presumably.

entries.meaning: According to what people say or believe, though the speaker doubts it is true. ---
examples: The old house is supposedly haunted.
This cream supposedly makes you look ten years younger.
He was supposedly sick, but I saw him at the game.
entries.type: stance — what people say, with doubt
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.form: -ly from supposed; the -ed is a full syllable: /zɪd/
entries.contrast: Supposedly signals that the speaker doubts the claim (якобы), unlike presumably (the speaker believes it). The form supposably is heard but counts as an error.

entries.meaning: According to what has been reported, though it is not confirmed. ---
examples: The singer is reportedly planning a world tour.
Reportedly, the two companies have been in talks for months.
The storm reportedly left thousands without power.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front with a comma
entries.form: -ly from reported; the -ed is a full syllable
entries.contrast: Reportedly only says the news comes from reports and is not confirmed; allegedly says someone has been accused of something.

examples: It was a seemingly simple question, but nobody could answer it.
We waited in a seemingly endless line of cars.
The seemingly quiet town had a lot of secrets.
Seemingly, nobody noticed the mistake.
The two men were seemingly unaware of each other.

senses.head: Appearing to be something, especially when this may not be true
examples: It was a seemingly simple question, but nobody could answer it.
We waited in a seemingly endless line of cars.
The seemingly quiet town had a lot of secrets.

senses.head: As far as anyone can tell; apparently
examples: Seemingly, nobody noticed the mistake.
The two men were seemingly unaware of each other.

entries.position: before its word — usually before an adjective; also front with a comma, or mid
entries.contrast: Before an adjective, seemingly hints that the look is false: a seemingly simple question = казалось бы, простой вопрос. At the front it is closer to apparently: Seemingly, nobody noticed = судя по всему, никто не заметил.

entries.meaning: Used to say that something good happened, or something bad was avoided, by good luck. ---
examples: Fortunately, no one was hurt in the accident.
We fortunately had an umbrella in the car.
Fortunately for us, the store was still open.
entries.type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid, or end after a comma

entries.meaning: Used to say that something is bad news or not what you wanted. ---
examples: Unfortunately, the concert is sold out.
I unfortunately won't be able to make it on Friday.
The package went to the wrong address, unfortunately.
entries.type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid, or end after a comma
entries.contrast: Unfortunately is the everyday English for к сожалению — in emails, refusals and bad news. Regrettably is formal and official, sadly adds real emotion, and to my regret sounds stiff.

entries.meaning: Used to say that something good happened because of good luck. ---
examples: Luckily, I had my phone with me.
We luckily found a parking spot right outside.
Luckily for him, the police officer let him go with a warning.
entries.type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid
entries.form: -ly from lucky, with y changed to i

examples: Sadly, the old theater was torn down in 2015.
Her grandfather sadly passed away last spring.
Sadly, the museum is closed on Mondays.
She smiled sadly and waved goodbye.
He shook his head sadly.
If you think I'll pay for that, you're sadly mistaken.
The old park has been sadly neglected.

senses.head: Used to say that something is sad or regrettable; unfortunately
examples: Sadly, the old theater was torn down in 2015.
Her grandfather sadly passed away last spring.
Sadly, the museum is closed on Mondays.

senses.head: In a sad way
examples: She smiled sadly and waved goodbye.
He shook his head sadly.

senses.head: Very much or completely, in a bad way — before a few adjectives and participles
examples: If you think I'll pay for that, you're sadly mistaken.
The old park has been sadly neglected.

entries.type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it; also manner and degree
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; end or mid in the manner sense; before its word in the degree sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense only (more sadly); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.modifies: clauses, verbs, adjectives and participles (sadly mistaken)
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Sadly, she left = к сожалению, она ушла; She left sadly = она ушла грустная. Sadly mistaken is degree: “very wrong”, with no sadness at all.

examples: Regrettably, we are unable to offer you a position at this time.
The event has regrettably been canceled.
Regrettably few students signed up for the program.
The city's response to the flooding was regrettably slow.

senses.head: Used in formal speech or writing to say that something is unfortunate
examples: Regrettably, we are unable to offer you a position at this time.
The event has regrettably been canceled.

senses.head: To a degree that is a pity — before an adjective or quantifier
examples: Regrettably few students signed up for the program.
The city's response to the flooding was regrettably slow.

entries.type: stance — the speaker's feeling about it; also degree
entries.position: front — with a comma; mid; before its word in the degree sense
entries.form: -ably from regret, with the t doubled
entries.contrast: Regrettably means “it is a pity”; regretfully means “with regret, feeling sorry” (She regretfully declined). Many Americans use regretfully for both, but careful writing keeps them apart. Regrettably is formal — in conversation say unfortunately.

examples: The food was amazingly good.
She handled the bad news amazingly well.
The tickets were amazingly cheap.
Amazingly, nobody was hurt in the crash.
The old car amazingly still runs.
Even more amazingly, the dog found its way home.

senses.head: To a very great or surprising degree; extremely
examples: The food was amazingly good.
She handled the bad news amazingly well.
The tickets were amazingly cheap.

senses.head: Used to say that something is very surprising
examples: Amazingly, nobody was hurt in the crash.
The old car amazingly still runs.
Even more amazingly, the dog found its way home.

entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb; front with a comma as a stance adverb
entries.comparison: more/most — even more amazingly, at the front
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Amazingly, she sang well = удивительно, что она хорошо спела; She sang amazingly well = она пела потрясающе.

examples: The test was surprisingly easy.
The hotel was surprisingly cheap for Manhattan.
He took the news surprisingly well.
Surprisingly, the youngest runner won the race.
Not surprisingly, the plan failed.
Most surprisingly, nobody complained about the price.

senses.head: To a degree that you would not expect
examples: The test was surprisingly easy.
The hotel was surprisingly cheap for Manhattan.
He took the news surprisingly well.

senses.head: Used to say that a fact or event is not what you expected
examples: Surprisingly, the youngest runner won the race.
Not surprisingly, the plan failed.
Most surprisingly, nobody complained about the price.

entries.position: before its word — before an adjective or adverb; front with a comma as a stance adverb
entries.comparison: more/most — even more surprisingly, most surprisingly, at the front
entries.contrast: False friend: Russian неожиданно often means “suddenly” (Неожиданно он встал) — that is suddenly, not surprisingly. Surprisingly only says the fact was not expected. Not surprisingly at the front means “as expected”.

examples: Thankfully, the rain stopped before the wedding.
The surgery was thankfully a success.
Thankfully, nobody was home when the tree fell.
He smiled thankfully at the nurse.
She sank thankfully into the hot bath.

senses.head: Used to say you are glad and relieved that something happened or did not happen
examples: Thankfully, the rain stopped before the wedding.
The surgery was thankfully a success.
Thankfully, nobody was home when the tree fell.

senses.head: In a grateful way
examples: He smiled thankfully at the nurse.
She sank thankfully into the hot bath.

entries.русский: к счастью, слава богу; с благодарностью
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid or end in the manner sense
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Thankfully, he took the money = слава богу, он взял деньги; He took the money thankfully = взял деньги с благодарностью. The stance use is standard American English.

examples: Ironically, the fire station burned down.
The anti-smoking ad was, ironically, paid for by a tobacco company.
Ironically, the more he tried to relax, the more stressed he got.
“Great job,” he said ironically, looking at the broken vase.
She smiled ironically when he called it a small problem.

senses.head: Used to say that something happened in the opposite way to what you would expect, in a strange or funny way
examples: Ironically, the fire station burned down.
The anti-smoking ad was, ironically, paid for by a tobacco company.
Ironically, the more he tried to relax, the more stressed he got.

senses.head: In an ironic way, meaning the opposite of what you say
examples: “Great job,” he said ironically, looking at the broken vase.
She smiled ironically when he called it a small problem.

entries.type: stance — an unexpected reversal; also manner
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — even more ironically, most ironically, at the front; more ironically in the manner sense
entries.contrast: Strictly, ironically needs a result opposite to what you would expect (по иронии судьбы); Americans often use it loosely for any coincidence or bad luck, which careful writers dislike.

examples: Predictably, the kids got bored after ten minutes.
Gas prices, predictably, went up before the holiday weekend.
The proposal was predictably rejected by the board.
The movie ended predictably, with a big wedding.
The new software behaves more predictably than the old version.

senses.head: Used to say that something happened exactly as people expected
examples: Predictably, the kids got bored after ten minutes.
Gas prices, predictably, went up before the holiday weekend.
The proposal was predictably rejected by the board.

senses.head: In a way that can be predicted, often too easily
examples: The movie ended predictably, with a big wedding.
The new software behaves more predictably than the old version.

entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid before a verb or adjective (predictably dull); end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more predictably); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Predictably, he lost = как и следовало ожидать, он проиграл; He played predictably = он играл предсказуемо.

examples: The cat watched the puppy curiously.
She looked at me curiously, as if trying to remember my name.
Curiously, nobody heard the alarm.
Curiously enough, the letter had no return address.
The street was curiously empty for a Saturday night.
He seemed curiously calm after the accident.

senses.head: In a way that shows you want to know about something
examples: The cat watched the puppy curiously.
She looked at me curiously, as if trying to remember my name.

senses.head: Used to say that a fact is strange or hard to explain
examples: Curiously, nobody heard the alarm.
Curiously enough, the letter had no return address.

senses.head: Strangely, in a way that is hard to explain — before an adjective
examples: The street was curiously empty for a Saturday night.
He seemed curiously calm after the accident.

entries.type: stance — something odd; also manner and degree
entries.position: end — in the manner sense; front with a comma as a stance adverb; before its word before an adjective
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more curiously); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: She asked about him curiously = спросила с любопытством; Curiously, she asked about him = странно, что она спросила. It is not курьёзно (funny, absurd).

entries.meaning: Used to say that a feeling or reaction is natural and easy to understand. ---
examples: She was understandably upset about losing her job.
Understandably, many parents are worried about the new policy.
He's understandably nervous before the surgery.
entries.русский: что вполне понятно, по понятным причинам
entries.position: mid — before the adjective or main verb, after be; also front with a comma
entries.contrast: Understandably does not mean “in a way that is easy to understand” (понятно объяснить = explain clearly). It means “and it is easy to see why”: She was understandably upset = она расстроилась, что вполне понятно.

examples: Hopefully, we'll be home before dark.
The package should hopefully arrive by Friday.
“Will it be fixed soon?” “Hopefully.”
The dog looked up at me hopefully.
She glanced hopefully at her phone.

senses.head: Used to say what you hope will happen
examples: Hopefully, we'll be home before dark.
The package should hopefully arrive by Friday.
“Will it be fixed soon?” “Hopefully.”

senses.head: In a hopeful way
examples: The dog looked up at me hopefully.
She glanced hopefully at her phone.

entries.type: stance — the speaker's hope; also manner
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; also mid; end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more hopefully); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.contrast: Russian speakers tend to say I hope every time; Hopefully is the natural spoken choice and fully standard in American English. Position changes the meaning: Hopefully, he'll call = надеюсь, он позвонит; He looked at the phone hopefully = он с надеждой смотрел на телефон.

entries.meaning: Used to introduce a fact that the speaker finds interesting or unexpected. ---
examples: Interestingly, the town has more dogs than people.
Interestingly enough, she never learned to drive.
The study, interestingly, found no link between the two.
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid after a comma
entries.contrast: Interestingly introduces a fact; it is not a reply like Интересно! (say Interesting! or That's interesting), and it never means “I wonder”: Интересно, придёт ли он = I wonder if he'll come.

examples: Naturally, we want the best for our kids.
He was naturally disappointed with the result.
“Are you coming to the wedding?” “Naturally.”
Her hair is naturally curly.
Some people are just naturally good at math.
Public speaking doesn't come naturally to me.
The cut will heal naturally in a few days.
Radon is a naturally occurring gas.
Try to smile naturally for the camera.
After a year in Chicago, she speaks English more naturally.

senses.head: Used to say that something is expected or normal; of course
examples: Naturally, we want the best for our kids.
He was naturally disappointed with the result.
“Are you coming to the wedding?” “Naturally.”

senses.head: Because of the qualities someone or something is born with
examples: Her hair is naturally curly.
Some people are just naturally good at math.
Public speaking doesn't come naturally to me.

senses.head: By nature, without chemicals, medicine or other outside help
examples: The cut will heal naturally in a few days.
Radon is a naturally occurring gas.

senses.head: In a relaxed, normal way that is not forced
examples: Try to smile naturally for the camera.
After a year in Chicago, she speaks English more naturally.

entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid; end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more naturally); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Naturally, she smiled = конечно, она улыбнулась; She smiled naturally = она улыбнулась непринуждённо. In Just act natural, Americans use the adjective, not naturally.

examples: Frankly, I don't care what he thinks.
The service was, frankly, terrible.
Quite frankly, the plan is a disaster.
She spoke frankly about her struggle with depression.
Can I talk to you frankly for a minute?

senses.head: Used to show that you are giving your honest opinion, even if it is not welcome
examples: Frankly, I don't care what he thinks.
The service was, frankly, terrible.
Quite frankly, the plan is a disaster.

senses.head: In an open and honest way
examples: She spoke frankly about her struggle with depression.
Can I talk to you frankly for a minute?

entries.type: stance — how it is being said; also manner
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; also mid after a comma; end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more frankly); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.contrast: Frankly usually warns that a blunt or critical opinion is coming, so it is sharper than откровенно говоря. Frankly speaking is understood but sounds non-native in American English — say Frankly or To be honest.

examples: Honestly, I don't remember what I said.
I honestly thought the store was open.
“Did you like the movie?” “Honestly? Not really.”
He made his money honestly.
Please answer every question honestly.
Honestly, can't you ever be on time?
Oh, honestly — who leaves the milk out all night?

senses.head: Used to stress that you are telling the truth or giving your real opinion
examples: Honestly, I don't remember what I said.
I honestly thought the store was open.
“Did you like the movie?” “Honestly? Not really.”

senses.head: In an honest way, without lying or cheating
examples: He made his money honestly.
Please answer every question honestly.

senses.head: Used to show that you are annoyed or disapprove
examples: Honestly, can't you ever be on time?
Oh, honestly — who leaves the milk out all night?

entries.type: stance — how it is being said; also manner
entries.position: front — with a comma as a stance adverb; mid before a verb (I honestly thought); end in the manner sense
entries.comparison: more/most — in the manner sense (more honestly); not gradable as a stance adverb
entries.form: -ly from honest; the h is silent
entries.contrast: Position changes the meaning: Honestly, I don't know comments on what you are saying (честно говоря, не знаю); Answer the questions honestly describes how (отвечайте честно). At the front with an annoyed tone, Honestly! means “ну честное слово!”.

examples: You need to take your health more seriously.
We're seriously thinking about moving to Texas.
Nobody took his threats seriously.
Two people were seriously injured in the crash.
Her father is seriously ill.
Seriously, though, are you okay?
You spent $500 on sneakers? Seriously?
That pizza was seriously good.
I'm seriously tired of this weather.

senses.head: In a serious way, with careful thought and not as a joke
examples: You need to take your health more seriously.
We're seriously thinking about moving to Texas.
Nobody took his threats seriously.

senses.head: Badly; to a dangerous degree
examples: Two people were seriously injured in the crash.
Her father is seriously ill.

senses.head: Used to show you mean what you say, or, as a question, to ask whether someone really means it
examples: Seriously, though, are you okay?
You spent $500 on sneakers? Seriously?

senses.head: Informal: very, really
examples: That pizza was seriously good.
I'm seriously tired of this weather.

entries.type: stance — speaking in earnest; also manner and degree
entries.position: end — in the manner sense (take it seriously); before its word in the degree sense; front with a comma as a stance adverb
entries.modifies: verbs, adjectives and participles (seriously injured), clauses
entries.contrast: Seriously ill or seriously injured means тяжело болен, тяжело ранен — nothing about attitude. In American speech Seriously? means “Are you kidding me?” (Да ладно?), often with annoyance.

entries.meaning: Used to admit that something is true, usually before a point that goes against it. ---
examples: Admittedly, the hotel was expensive, but the view was worth it.
The movie was, admittedly, a bit too long.
It's admittedly not a perfect solution, but it will work for now.
entries.position: front — with a comma; also mid
entries.form: -ly from admitted; the -ed is a full syllable
entries.contrast: Admittedly concedes a weak point and is normally followed by but. It does not mean по общему признанию (widely recognized) — that is by all accounts or widely.

examples: The two phones are basically the same.
Her story is basically true, though she left out some details.
He's basically a nice guy.
Basically, we ran out of money.
So basically, you're telling me I'm fired?
I'm basically done — just a few emails left.
He basically lives at his girlfriend's apartment.

senses.head: In the most important ways; fundamentally
examples: The two phones are basically the same.
Her story is basically true, though she left out some details.
He's basically a nice guy.

senses.head: Used to sum something up in a simple way
examples: Basically, we ran out of money.
So basically, you're telling me I'm fired?

senses.head: Almost completely; practically
examples: I'm basically done — just a few emails left.
He basically lives at his girlfriend's apartment.

entries.русский: по сути, в основном; в общем; практически
entries.type: stance — summing up or simplifying; also degree
entries.position: mid — before the main verb or adjective, after be; front with a comma when summing up
entries.contrast: Russian в принципе is often in principle (in theory), not basically: In principle I agree, but…. Used as a filler in every sentence, basically sounds sloppy, especially in writing.

examples: The restaurant looks small, but it's actually pretty big inside.
What actually happened that night?
I actually enjoyed the movie more than the book.
“You're from Ohio, right?” “Actually, I'm from Indiana.”
Actually, that's not quite what I said.
Actually, I'll have the salmon instead.
Actually, could you pick up some milk on the way home?
He actually apologized — I couldn't believe it.
The kids actually cleaned their rooms without being asked.

senses.head: In fact; really — often in contrast to what was expected or what seems true
examples: The restaurant looks small, but it's actually pretty big inside.
What actually happened that night?
I actually enjoyed the movie more than the book.

senses.head: Used to correct someone or to disagree politely
examples: “You're from Ohio, right?” “Actually, I'm from Indiana.”
Actually, that's not quite what I said.

senses.head: Used when you change your mind or add a new request
examples: Actually, I'll have the salmon instead.
Actually, could you pick up some milk on the way home?

senses.head: Used to show that something is surprising
examples: He actually apologized — I couldn't believe it.
The kids actually cleaned their rooms without being asked.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; front with a comma when correcting
entries.contrast: False friend: actually never means актуально (relevant, up to date — say relevant or current), and actual is not актуальный. В настоящее время is currently, not actually.

examples: He literally lives next door to his boss.
There were literally thousands of people in the square.
Don't take everything he says so literally.
The name literally means “red river.”
You can't translate this idiom literally.
I literally died laughing.
My phone is literally glued to my hand.

senses.head: In the real, exact sense of the words, not as an exaggeration
examples: He literally lives next door to his boss.
There were literally thousands of people in the square.
Don't take everything he says so literally.

senses.head: Word for word, in a translation or explanation of a name
examples: The name literally means “red river.”
You can't translate this idiom literally.

senses.head: Informal: used for emphasis, even when the words are not really true
examples: I literally died laughing.
My phone is literally glued to my hand.

entries.type: stance — exactness of the words; also degree
entries.position: mid — before the main verb or the word it stresses; end in the translation sense
entries.contrast: Informal literally for emphasis (I literally died laughing) is very common but annoys many listeners; in writing keep it for things that are really true. Take something literally = понимать буквально.

examples: The results were indeed impressive.
“Is this your car?” “It is indeed.”
We did indeed receive your letter.
The plan is risky; indeed, it may be impossible.
Many students, indeed most of them, passed the test.
Thank you very much indeed.
It was a very good meal indeed.
“Why would anyone do that?” “Why indeed?”
“Who's paying for all this?” “Who indeed.”

senses.head: Used to confirm or agree that something is true
examples: The results were indeed impressive.
“Is this your car?” “It is indeed.”
We did indeed receive your letter.

senses.head: Used to add a stronger point to what was just said
examples: The plan is risky; indeed, it may be impossible.
Many students, indeed most of them, passed the test.

senses.head: Used after very and an adjective or adverb for extra emphasis
examples: Thank you very much indeed.
It was a very good meal indeed.

senses.head: Used to repeat a question and show that you also wonder about it, or find it odd
examples: “Why would anyone do that?” “Why indeed?”
“Who's paying for all this?” “Who indeed.”

entries.type: stance — confirming or strengthening; also linking and degree
entries.position: mid — after be and the first auxiliary; after its word in very … indeed; front before a stronger point
entries.modifies: clauses, verbs, very + adjective or adverb
entries.form: in + deed, written as one word
entries.contrast: Indeed is formal in American English; in conversation really or yes is more natural, and very good indeed sounds British. A surprised Действительно? is Really?, not Indeed?.

examples: You have doubtless heard the news by now.
He will doubtless complain about the price.
It was doubtless the right decision.
Her talent is doubtless real, but she needs more practice.

senses.head: Very probably; the speaker is fairly sure
examples: You have doubtless heard the news by now.
He will doubtless complain about the price.

senses.head: Without doubt; certainly
examples: It was doubtless the right decision.
Her talent is doubtless real, but she needs more practice.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; also front
entries.form: -less, with no -ly (doubtlessly exists but is rarer)
entries.contrast: Despite its look, doubtless often means only “probably”: You have doubtless heard the news = вы, наверное, уже слышали. For full certainty use undoubtedly or without a doubt. It is formal and mostly written.

examples: The two plans are essentially the same.
She is essentially a shy person.
The rules have stayed essentially unchanged since 1990.
The work is essentially finished — we just need to paint.
Essentially, what he's saying is no.

senses.head: In the most basic and important way; fundamentally
examples: The two plans are essentially the same.
She is essentially a shy person.
The rules have stayed essentially unchanged since 1990.

senses.head: In effect; almost completely
examples: The work is essentially finished — we just need to paint.
Essentially, what he's saying is no.

entries.position: mid — before the main verb or adjective, after be; front with a comma when summing up
entries.contrast: False friend: essentially is not существенно (considerably): Prices rose significantly, not essentially. It means “in essence”, and is a more formal basically.

examples: It was a truly beautiful wedding.
The view from the top is truly amazing.
I'm truly sorry for your loss.
She truly loves her job.
Nobody truly understands how the brain works.
Is he truly happy, or just pretending?

senses.head: Really; to a very great degree — before an adjective
examples: It was a truly beautiful wedding.
The view from the top is truly amazing.

senses.head: Sincerely; with real feeling
examples: I'm truly sorry for your loss.
She truly loves her job.

senses.head: In fact and completely, not just in name or appearance
examples: Nobody truly understands how the brain works.
Is he truly happy, or just pretending?

entries.type: stance — sincerity and emphasis; also degree
entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; mid before a verb
entries.form: -ly from true, dropping the e; never truely
entries.contrast: Truly is more formal and emotional than really. Yours truly at the end of a letter is formal (искренне ваш); in speech yours truly is a fixed phrase that jokingly means “me” (ваш покорный слуга).

examples: She genuinely cares about her students.
I was genuinely happy for him.
He seemed genuinely surprised by the party.
This is a genuinely new approach to the problem.
Is the painting genuinely old, or is it a copy?

senses.head: With real feeling; sincerely
examples: She genuinely cares about her students.
I was genuinely happy for him.
He seemed genuinely surprised by the party.

senses.head: Really, and not just seeming to be
examples: This is a genuinely new approach to the problem.
Is the painting genuinely old, or is it a copy?

entries.position: before its word — before an adjective; mid before a verb
entries.contrast: Pronunciation trap: the last syllable of genuine is /ɪn/, not /aɪn/ like wine, so genuinely is JEN-yoo-in-lee.

examples: She'll likely be late again.
Most likely, the flight will be delayed.
Prices will more than likely go up next year.
entries.position: mid — before the main verb, after be and the first auxiliary; most likely also front
entries.comparison: more/most — more likely, most likely; also more than likely and very likely
entries.form: flat — the same form as the adjective likely (a likely result)
entries.contrast: Word-class trap: in He is likely to win, likely is an adjective (with to); the adverb has no to: He will likely win. US/UK split: bare He'll likely win is normal American English, while British English prefers He'll probably win or most likely.
